note: South Carolina has a division specifically for this: Out of Home Abuse and Neglect, inside the Department of Social Services, which handles abuse and neglect of people in facilities rather than in family homes. That is the right first call for something that happened inside a program, and it has its own daytime and after-hours numbers.

civil_injury.summary: Three years for assault, battery or injury from negligence, counted from when you knew or should have known you had a claim. False imprisonment has a shorter two-year deadline.
civil_injury.quote: Within three years: ... (5) an action for assault, battery, or any injury to the person or rights of another, not arising on contract and not enumerated by law
civil_injury.note: 15-3-535: actions under 15-3-530(5) 'must be commenced within three years after the person knew or by the exercise of reasonable diligence should have known that he had a cause of action.' 15-3-550: 'Within two years: (1) an action for libel, slander, or false imprisonment'.

civil_minor_tolling.summary: Time spent under 18 does not count, but the extra time can never go past one year after your 18th birthday. So a person hurt as a child has at least until age 19, or longer if the normal three years from the injury (or from discovery) ends later.
civil_minor_tolling.quote: the time of the disability is not a part of the time limited for the commencement of the action, except that the period within which the action must be brought cannot be extended: (a) more than five years by any such disability, except infancy; nor (b) in any case longer than one year after the ...
civil_minor_tolling.note: Applies to Article 5 actions (which include 15-3-530 and 15-3-550) and Tort Claims Act actions. The cap limits only the extension; it does not appear to cut short the normal period, but that reading was not confirmed against case law. The discovery rule in 15-3-535 applies to all 15-3-530(5) claims and may help survivors who did not connect their injury to the abuse until later. No extended period for non-sexual child abuse was found.

civil_government_claims.summary: Claims against the state or a county, city or other local government under the Tort Claims Act must be filed in court within two years of when the loss was or should have been discovered, or within three years if a verified claim was first filed with the agency (that claim is due within one year). Being a minor extends this under the rule above.
civil_government_claims.quote: Except as provided for in Section 15-3-40, any action brought pursuant to this chapter is forever barred unless an action is commenced within two years after the date the loss was or should have been discovered
civil_government_claims.note: Filing a verified claim is optional ('may be filed'); if filed, 15-78-80(d) says it 'must be received within one year after the loss was or should have been discovered', and the lawsuit deadline becomes three years.

criminal_child_abuse.summary: No time limit. South Carolina has no general statute of limitations for crimes, so child abuse can be charged at any time.
criminal_child_abuse.citation: No statute; South Carolina has no general criminal statute of limitations
criminal_child_abuse.quote: There is no statute of limitations in South Carolina, and prosecution can resume if new evidence supporting the charge comes to light.
criminal_child_abuse.note: Source is the 14th Circuit Solicitor's Office (a South Carolina prosecutor's office), not statute text: the rule is the absence of any statute, so there is no section to quote. A very long delay can still be challenged as a due process violation (pre-indictment delay; see State v. Brazell, 325 S.C. 65 (1997)). A few specific statutes outside Title 16 set their own limits (for example some tax and election offenses), none found for child abuse or assault.

criminal_felony_assault.summary: No time limit for felony or misdemeanor assault. South Carolina has no general statute of limitations for crimes.
criminal_felony_assault.citation: No statute; South Carolina has no general criminal statute of limitations
criminal_felony_assault.quote: There is no statute of limitations in South Carolina, and prosecution can resume if new evidence supporting the charge comes to light.
criminal_felony_assault.note: Same basis as criminal_child_abuse. Could not locate a South Carolina appellate opinion quoting the rule in the time available; the rule is widely stated but was confirmed here only from a prosecutor's office publication.

channels.name: South Carolina Department of Labor, Licensing and Regulation, Office of Investigations and Enforcement
channels.what_it_can_do: Investigates complaints against licensed professionals - including professional counselors, marriage and family therapists, psychologists and social workers - and against unlicensed people practising a profession that requires a licence, to decide whether the facts alleged could breach the law regulating that profession.
channels.who_to_report: Any licensed mental health professional in South Carolina, or somebody practising without the licence.
channels.how: Use the online complaint system, or call. State the facts briefly and clearly, give the name, address and phone number of every witness and what each of them knows, and attach any documents, records, statements or contracts that help.
channels.phone_note: Complaints. The Counselors board direct line is 803-896-4658.
channels.mail: SC Department of Labor, Licensing and Regulation, 110 Centerview Dr, Columbia, SC 29210
channels.note: The Department puts the burden on you: it says the complaining party is responsible for making sure everything needed is on the form.

channels.name: South Carolina DSS, Out of Home Abuse and Neglect (OHAN)
channels.what_it_can_do: The Department of Social Services division that investigates abuse and neglect of people living in facilities, as distinct from abuse in a family home.
channels.who_to_report: A young person abused or neglected inside a South Carolina facility. This is the right first call for something that happened in a program.
channels.how: Call the daytime line during office hours, or the after-hours number outside them.

channels.name: South Carolina child abuse and neglect hotline
channels.what_it_can_do: The Department of Social Services 24-hour line for reporting suspected child abuse or neglect.
channels.who_to_report: A child at a South Carolina program. For abuse inside a facility, Out of Home Abuse and Neglect is the more specific route.
channels.phone_note: 1-888-CARE4US. 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

channels.name: Disability Rights South Carolina
channels.what_it_can_do: South Carolina's Protection and Advocacy agency, with federal authority to investigate abuse and neglect of people with disabilities in facilities, a right of access to them, and free legal advocacy. It publishes its own guide to reporting abuse in a facility, naming each agency.
channels.who_to_report: A South Carolina program where the young person has a disability or a mental health diagnosis.
channels.how: Contact the intake line, or start from its reporting guide.

channels.name: South Carolina DSS child care and residential licensing
channels.what_it_can_do: Sets the licensing standards for child care and group care facilities in South Carolina, inspects against them, investigates complaints and takes enforcement action. On receiving a regulatory complaint it must carry out an unannounced inspection of the facility.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed facility, where the problem is a regulatory breach rather than a specific allegation of abuse.
channels.how: File through the Department's complaint route. A complaint alleging immediate danger to children is investigated within 24 to 48 hours.
channels.note: The unannounced inspection is the point: a regulatory complaint forces the state through the door without warning.
